facts.claim: "Montana" was written by Pierce Edens and is the opening track of his self-titled 2012 album.
The self-titled album was produced by Adam Johnson and Pierce Edens, and engineered and mastered by Adam Johnson, as a SoundLab Studios production.
Album credits list Pierce Edens on vocals, guitar, banjo and percussion; Ron Clearfield on cello; Jesse James Hongisto on bass; Lady Lane on backup vocals; and Nicky Sanders on violin.
The album was recorded at Edens' renovated childhood home in the Appalachian Mountains of Western North Carolina.
Edens bought his family home and remodeled it as a recording space, and the album was recorded there in 2012 with The Dirty Work.
The album was fan-financed through Kickstarter, which raised 130 percent of its goal within 45 days.
The album moved away from the 'bar-band, rockabilly blues' style of The Dirty Work toward a folk-oriented singer-songwriter approach. It adds a string section, background vocals and heavy overdubs.
Indy Week said the punk influence shows in the rebellious, free-spirited nature of 'Montana'.
A live version, 'Montana: Live', was released as a single in December 2013.
Edens is an Asheville, NC singer-songwriter who grew up on regional mountain folk, then got into punk and grunge as a teenager. He merged the two styles, and self-released the Four Songs EP in 2004.

draft:
The plan in **Montana** is half-baked on purpose. Pierce Edens wants to trade his truck for horses when he gets there and tear down every fence he meets, and he admits the logistics are an afterthought: "we work the details later / if we work them out at all." That shrug is the most honest line in the song. It tells you this isn't a relocation plan. It's a way of saying *let's not be here anymore* to someone you hope will say yes.

The trouble with here comes in sideways. Two angels show up in a dream to warn that "this whole town is going under," and later the narrator sounds worn out on the place itself. The old story keeps coming around "again," and he swears one more hearing will make him snap. "We've been beat so down," he says, before adding the brag that they "painted this whole town." Pride and exhaustion sit in the same breath. He had a good time here, and it's done with him. Montana is barely a place in the song. It's a big sky, back roads and no fences, all of it borrowed from Western movies, and Edens knows it.

The phrase he keeps landing on is "Just be happy lonesome and free." It's a strange wish to make to someone you're begging to come along. Lonesome usually means without anyone. Here it means alone together, two people off the map, and "You and me" gets repeated until it reads as a promise he's trying to make true by saying it.

The music doesn't hurry him. Strummed acoustic guitar, a walking bass line and a simple kit beat settle into a relaxed country shuffle at a moderate pace. The sound is dry and close, with nothing between the band and the listener. Edens sings in a clear voice with a little rasp at the edges, and his delivery stays conversational, like he's making the pitch across the cab of the truck rather than from a stage.

The backstory adds a twist. Edens grew up on mountain folk in Western North Carolina, then got into punk and grunge as a teenager, and Indy Week heard that punk streak in this song's rebellious, free-spirited pull. The self-titled album it opens was fan-funded on Kickstarter and recorded in his childhood home in the Appalachians, which he bought and turned into a studio. So a song about leaving town for good was cut in the house he came back to, a contradiction the song leaves alone.

It sticks because it captures the moment just before you leave anywhere, when the escape still feels like freedom and you're still waiting to hear whether you'll make it alone.
